source_text: «δημιουργός» καί «ἐξουσιαστής» καί «τῆς εἰρήνης αὐτοῦ οὐκ ἔστιν ὅριον» καί «σωτήρ» καί «πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν Χριστός» καί «εὐλογημένος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας» καὶ ὅτι «μέγα τὸ τῆς εὐσεβείας μυστήριον» δῆλον δ' ὡς τὸ Χριστιανῶν, παρ' οἷς ἀγένητος θεὸς ὑμνεῖται ὁ Χριστός καὶ ὅτι τῇ ἑαυτοῦ θεότητι «περιποιεῖ τὸν λαόν», διὰ τὸ ὁμοουσίως ἔχειν πρὸς τὸν πατέρα. 27.2 Τοιῶσδε τοίνυν περὶ τούτων λέγουσιν οἱ μνημονευθησόμενοι νῦν πρὸς ἡμῶν ἅγιοι, οἷς ὁ θεὸς κατὰ τὸν ιεʹ ψαλμόν «ἐγνώρισεν ὁδοὺς ζωῆς»· 27.3 ∆αυῒδ ἐν μὲν ζʹ ψαλμῷ εὐχόμενος· «ἐξεγέρθητι, κύριε ὁ θεός μου, ἐν προστάγματι, ᾧ ἐνετείλω, καὶ συναγωγὴ λαῶν κυκλώσει σε, καὶ ὑπὲρ ταύτης εἰς ὕψος ἐπίστρεψον». 27.4 αἰσθάνῃ, ὡς ὁ προφήτης κύριον καὶ θεὸν οἶδεν αὐτὸν καὶ δέεται αὐτοῦ λέγων «ἐξεγέρθητι» ἐπὶ τὴν ἀνεκλάλητον ἐνανθρώπησίν σου, τρόπῳ ᾧ προώρισας τῷ «λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον, καὶ ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις ἐγερῶ αὐτόν». 27.5 ὑπὲρ ταύτης γάρ φησιν τῆς· περιγινομένης ἡμῖν ἐντεῦθεν σωτηρίας· «τὰ μὲν ἔθνη τῇ πίστει κυκλώσει σε· σὺ δέ, ὅθεν ἦλθες, ἀχωρίστως ἐπάνελθε»· 27.6 ἐν δὲ μϛʹ· «θεὸς μέγας κύριος καὶ βασιλεὺς μέγας ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν». ἐν δὲ μθʹ· «ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν ἡλίου μέχρι δυσμῶν ἐκ Σιὼν ἡ εὐπρέπεια τῆς ὡραιότητος αὐτοῦ· ὁ θεὸς ἐμφανῶς ἥξει»· ἐν δὲ ξζʹ· «ἀναστήτω ὁ θεός, καὶ διασκορπισθήτωσαν οἱ ἐχθροὶ αὐτοῦ» καί «ὁδοποιήσατε τῷ ἐπιβεβηκότι ἐπὶ δυσμάς· κύριος ὄνομα αὐτῷ» ἐν δὲ παʹ· «ἀνάστα, ὁ θεός, κρῖνον τὴν γῆν». 27.7 Ἄθρει μέν, πῶς ἑκάστη λέξις ἀνάπτει τὴν περὶ αὐτοῦ δόξαν καὶ ἐξαρκεῖ πεῖσαι τῆς πατρικῆς μονάδος ὑπάρχειν αὐτὸν οὐσίας· καὶ ὅτι ὁ μεγαλογράφος τὸν ἐν τάφῳ οὐ δίχα ζωῆς τεθέντα, ἵνα σὺν τοῖς ζῶσιν καὶ τοὺς ἀπελθόντας τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων πραγμάτων σώσῃ, θεὸν καλεῖ καὶ ἀνίστασθαι τοῦ μνήματος προφητεύει κρινοῦντα τοὺς μετὰ τοσαύτην καὶ τηλικαύτην εὐεργεσίαν γηΐνως φρονήσαντας. 27.8 ἴσθι δέ, ὅτι «δυσμάς» τοὺς ἐσχάτους λέγει καιρούς. ἐν αὐτοῖς γὰρ ἐπέστη ἐμφανῶς τῷδε τῷ θεατῷ κόσμῳ. 27.9 Ἐν δὲ οϛʹ· «ἐν τῷ ἁγίῳ ἡ ὁδός σου. τίς θεὸς μέγας ὡς ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν; σὺ εἶ ὁ θεὸς ὁ ποι ῶν θαυμάσια μόνος». 27.10 τὸν σαρκωθέντα θεὸν λόγον ἀνευφημεῖ κἀνταῦθα τὸν ἐν τῷ Ἰουδαϊκῷ ἱερῷ ἐμφιλοχωρήσαντα καὶ διδάξαντα καὶ θαυματουργήσαντα· 27.11 Ἐν δὲ τῷ ριζʹ· «εὐλογημένος ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίου· θεὸς μέγας κύριος καὶ ἐπέ φανεν ἡμῖν». 27.12 εἰ εὐλόγως παρὰ τῷ προφήτῃ «θεὸς μέγας» καὶ εἰ «εὐλογημένος», ὅ ἐστιν δεδοξασμένος, καί «βασιλεὺς μέγας» καί «μόνος θαυματουργός» ὑπάρχει ὁ ἐπιφανεὶς ἡμῖν κύριος, ἔστιν δὲ ὁ υἱός, –ἀλόγως παρὰ αἱρετικοῖς μικρότερος τοῦ ἰδίου πατρὸς ὑπονοεῖται. 27.13 οὐκ ἐνδέχεται γὰρ τὸν αὐτὸν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ πρώτως μὲν ἔχειν κατὰ τὴν προφητείαν, δευτέρως δὲ κατ' ἐκείνους. 27.14 Εἰ δὴ πυθόμεθα τοῦ αὐτοῦ ψαλμῳδοῦ, μαθησόμεθα, ὅτι ἐπίσταται ὡς τὸν πατέρα οὕτω καὶ τὸν υἱὸν ὑπάρχοντα θεὸν τῶν προπατόρων. 27.15 ἐν γὰρ μϛʹ ψαλμῷ κέκραγεν· «ἐβασίλευσεν ὁ θεὸς ἐπὶ τὰ ἔθνη. ὁ θεὸς κάθηται ἐπὶ θρόνου ἁγίου αὐτοῦ· ἄρχοντες λαῶν 30 συνήχθησαν μετὰ τοῦ θεοῦ Ἀβραάμ». 27.16 συνεκκλησιάσθησαν δὲ μετὰ τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ἐνανθρωπήσαντος, περὶ οὗ ᾄδεται ἐν βʹ ψαλμῷ· «ἱνατί ἐφρύαξαν ἔθνη καὶ λαοὶ ἐμελέτησαν κενά; παρέστησαν οἱ βασιλεῖς τῆς γῆς καὶ οἱ ἄρχοντες συνήχθησαν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ κατὰ τοῦ κυρίου καὶ κατὰ τοῦ χριστοῦ αὐτοῦ». 27.17 Ἠσαΐας δὲ ἀσύγκριτον αὐτὸν ὡς τὸν θεὸν πατέρα βοᾷ· «ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος οὐκ ἠκούσαμεν οὐδὲ οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ ἡμῶν εἶδον θεὸν πλὴν σοῦ». 27.18 ἄλλον γὰρ οὐκ εἴδομεν θεὸν ἢ τὸν ἐκ παρθένου Μαρίας κατὰ τὴν σωτήριον ἐνανθρώπησιν τεχθέντα οὐδὲ ἠκούσαμεν, εἰ μὴ τὸν μαρτυρηθέντα ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ πατρός· 27.19 «οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός» 27.20 καὶ πάλιν, ὡς προελέχθη· «παιδίον ἐγεννήθη ἡμῖν, υἱὸς καὶ ἐδόθη, οὗ ἡ ἀρχὴ ἐπὶ τοῦ ὤμου αὐτοῦ· καὶ καλεῖται τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ θεὸς ἰσχυρός, ἐξουσιαστής, ἄρχων εἰρήνης, πατὴρ τοῦ μέλλοντος αἰῶνος». 27.21 μεθ' ἕτερά τε ἐπάγει· «καὶ τῆς εἰρήνης αὐτοῦ οὐκ ἔστιν ὅριον». 27.22 ὁ υἱός, φησίν, τοῦ θεοῦ ἐνανθρωπήσας ἐγεννήθη παιδίον καὶ ἐδόθη ἡμῖν φέρων αὐτὸς ἐπὶ τοῦ ὤμου αὐτοῦ ταύτης αὐτοῦ τῆς κάτω γεννήσεως τὴν ἀρχήν, τοῦτ' ἔστιν· αὐτὸς ἑαυτοῦ ἀρχὴ τυγχάνων ἐν τῷ ἀρεύστως ὑπὸ παρθένου καὶ ἐξ αὐτῆς ἀρρήτως σαρκωθέντα τεχθῆναι, συνουσίας ἀνδρὸς ἀρχὴν οὐ παρασχόμενος. 27.23 ὄνομα δὲ αὐτῷ· «θεὸς ἰσχυρός, ἐξουσιαστής». 27.24 οὐκ εἶπεν· «ὑπεξούσιος», ἀλλ' ἐφανέρωσεν αὐτοῦ τὴν φύσιν, τὴν δύναμιν, τὴν αὐθεντείαν. 27.25 Ὅπερ ὄνομα γινώσκων ∆αυῒδ pass_a_gloss: [... and] 'craftsman' and 'one holding authority' and 'of his peace there is no boundary' and 'saviour' and 'Christ all things in all' and 'blessed into the ages', and that 'great is the mystery of godliness', plainly that of Christians, among whom Christ is hymned as uncreated God, and that by his own deity 'he acquires the people', on account of being of the same being toward the Father. 27.2 In such a way then about these things speak the saints who will now be mentioned by us, to whom God according to the 15th psalm (English 16) 'made known ways of life'. 27.3 David in the 7th psalm praying: 'be roused, Lord my God, by the command which you commanded, and a gathering of peoples will encircle you, and on behalf of this return to the height'. 27.4 You perceive that the prophet knows him as Lord and God and begs him, saying 'be roused' to your unspeakable becoming man, in the manner which you marked out beforehand by the 'destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it'. 27.5 For 'on behalf of this' he says, of the salvation accruing to us from this: 'the nations will encircle you by the faith; and you, from where you came, return without separation'. 27.6 And in the 46th (English 47): 'a great God is Lord and a great king over all the earth'. And in the 49th (English 50): 'from risings of sun as far as settings, from Zion the comeliness of his beauty; God will come visibly'. And in the 67th (English 68): 'let God rise up, and let his enemies be scattered', and 'make a road for the one mounted upon the settings; Lord is name to him'. And in the 81st (English 82): 'rise up, God, judge the earth'. 27.7 Look how each word kindles the glory about him and suffices to persuade that he is of the being of the Father's oneness; and that the writer of great things calls God the one placed in the tomb not without life, so that with the living he might also save those who had gone away from human affairs, and prophesies him rising from the tomb to judge those who after so much and so great a benefaction thought in an earthly way. 27.8 And know that by 'settings' he means the last times; for in them he came upon this visible world visibly. 27.9 And in the 76th (English 77): 'in the holy is your way. Who is a great God like our God? You are the God who does wonders alone'. 27.10 Here too he hails the God Word made flesh, the one who lingered fondly in the Jewish temple and taught and worked wonders. 27.11 And in the 117th (English 118): 'blessed the one coming in the name of the Lord; a great God is Lord and appeared to us'. 27.12 If with good reason, in the prophet, the Lord who appeared to us is 'great God' and 'blessed', which is glorified, and 'great king' and 'only wonder-worker', and he is the Son, without reason among heretics is he suspected to be smaller than his own Father. 27.13 For it is not admissible for the same one in truth to hold first according to the prophecy, but second according to those. 27.14 If indeed we inquire of the same psalm-singer, we will learn that he understands the Son, as the Father, to be God of the forefathers. 27.15 For in the 46th psalm (English 47) he has cried: 'God reigned over the nations. God sits upon his holy throne; rulers of peoples were gathered with the God of Abraham'. 27.16 And they were assembled together with the God who became man, about whom it is sung in the 2nd psalm: 'why did nations snort and peoples practise empty things? The kings of the earth stood by and the rulers were gathered to the same place against the Lord and against his anointed'. 27.17 And Isaiah shouts him incomparable as God the Father: 'from the age we did not hear, nor did our eyes see a God except you'. 27.18 For we did not see another God than the one born from the virgin Mary according to the saving becoming man, nor did we hear, except the one witnessed by God the Father: 27.19 'this is my beloved Son', 27.20 and again, as was said before: 'a child was born to us, a son also was given, whose rule is upon his shoulder; and his name is called mighty God, one holding authority, ruler of peace, father of the coming age'. 27.21 And after other things he brings on: 'and of his peace there is no boundary'. 27.22 The Son of God, he says, having become man, was born a child and was given to us, himself carrying upon his shoulder the beginning of this lower birth of his, that is: he being himself his own beginning in being born without flux by a virgin and from her unspeakably made flesh, not having furnished a beginning from intercourse of a man. 27.23 And name to him: 'mighty God, one holding authority'. 27.24 He did not say 'under authority', but made manifest his nature, the power, the sovereign authority. 27.25 Which name knowing, David sings: 'let them know that name to you [...]
pass_b_english: “Creator,” and “Sovereign,” and “of his peace there is no bound” (Isaiah 9:7), and “Saviour,” and “Christ is all in all” (Colossians 3:11), and “blessed for ever” (Romans 9:5); and that “great is the mystery of godliness” (1 Timothy 3:16), plainly the mystery of the Christians, among whom Christ is hymned as uncreated God; and that by his own Godhead “he acquires the people,” because he is of one substance with the Father.

Such, then, is what the saints we shall now mention say on these matters, the saints to whom God, as Psalm 16 says, “made known the ways of life” (Psalm 16:11). David in Psalm 7 prays: “Arise, O Lord my God, by the command you gave, and an assembly of peoples shall surround you; and for its sake return on high” (Psalm 7:6-7). You see that the prophet knows him as Lord and God, and entreats him when he says “Arise”: arise to your ineffable incarnation, in the way you marked out beforehand when you said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). For by “for its sake” he means the salvation that comes to us from it: “The nations will surround you by faith; and you, return without separation to the place from which you came.”

And in Psalm 47: “The Lord is a great God, and a great King over all the earth” (Psalm 47:2). And in Psalm 50: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, out of Zion is the splendour of his beauty; God will come openly” (Psalm 50:1-3). And in Psalm 68: “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered” (Psalm 68:1), and “Make a way for him who rides upon the west; the Lord is his name” (Psalm 68:4). And in Psalm 82: “Arise, O God, judge the earth” (Psalm 82:8).

Observe how each word kindles his glory and is enough to persuade us that he is of the substance of the Father’s unity. Observe, too, that the writer of great things calls God the one who was laid in the tomb not without life, so that he might save, together with the living, those also who had departed from human affairs; and he prophesies that he rises from the grave to judge those who, after a kindness so great and so vast, set their minds on earthly things. Know that by “the west” he means the last times; for it was in them that he came openly into this visible world.

And in Psalm 77: “Your way is in the holy place. Who is a great God like our God? You are the God who alone works wonders” (Psalm 77:13-14). Here too he extols God the Word made flesh, who loved to linger in the Jewish temple, and taught there, and worked wonders.

And in Psalm 118: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; the Lord is a great God, and he has appeared to us” (Psalm 118:26-27). If it is with good reason that the Lord who appeared to us is, in the prophet, “a great God” and “blessed” (that is, glorified), and “great King” and “only worker of wonders,” and this is the Son, then it is without reason that the heretics suspect him of being less than his own Father. For it is not possible for one and the same being, in truth, to hold the first place according to the prophecy and the second according to them.

If we inquire of the same psalmist, we shall learn that he knows the Son, like the Father, to be the God of our forefathers. For in Psalm 47 he has cried out: “God reigns over the nations; God sits upon his holy throne. The rulers of the peoples were gathered with the God of Abraham” (Psalm 47:8-9). They assembled together with God made man, of whom it is sung in Psalm 2: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples plot vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers were gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Psalm 2:1-2).

Isaiah cries out that he, like God the Father, is beyond compare: “From of old we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen, a God besides you” (Isaiah 64:4). For we have seen no other God than the one born of the Virgin Mary in the saving incarnation; nor have we heard any other, except the one to whom God the Father bore witness: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17). And again, as was said before: “A child was born to us, a son also was given, whose rule is upon his shoulder; and his name is called Mighty God, Sovereign, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come” (Isaiah 9:6). And after other words he adds: “And of his peace there is no bound” (Isaiah 9:7).

The Son of God, he means, having become man, was born a child and was given to us, himself bearing upon his shoulder the rule, the very beginning, of this his birth here below. That is, he is himself his own beginning, in that he was born of a virgin without passion and was ineffably made flesh from her, while no union with a man supplied his beginning. And his name is “Mighty God, Sovereign.” He did not say “subject to authority”; he disclosed his nature, his power, his sovereign authority. choices.issue: Edition numbers printed, wrong Psalm numbers, misread numeral, garbled clauses, stray paragraph
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English printed edition numbers 27.12-27.25 in the reading text. It copied or misread the Greek Psalm numbers: Psalm '19' for ιεʹ (Greek 15 = Psalm 16), '67' for ζʹ (Psalm 7), '45' for μϛʹ (Greek 46 = Psalm 47), '44' for μθʹ (Greek 49 = Psalm 50), '67' for ξζʹ (Greek 67 = Psalm 68), '69' for παʹ (Greek 81 = Psalm 82), '69' for οϛʹ (Greek 76 = Psalm 77), '44th' for μϛʹ in 27.15 (Psalm 47); and it read ριζʹ (Greek 117 = Psalm 118) as 'Regarding the root'. Clauses fixed: 'unbegotten God' (ἀγένητος: uncreated), 'praised without words' (ἀνευφημεῖ: extols aloud), 'thought wisely' (γηΐνως φρονήσαντας: set their minds on earthly things), 'this spectacle has visibly appeared' (he came openly into this visible world), 'he exists as the essence of the Father's unity', 'one who has authority' (ὑπεξούσιος: subject to authority), 'not granting the rule of a man's union'. A stray paragraph 'And in' removed. References: 'Ps 47:8' made Psalm 47:8-9, 'Ps 2:2' made Psalm 2:1-2, 'Isa', 'Matt' written in full; Isaiah 9:7, Colossians 3:11, Romans 9:5, 1 Timothy 3:16, Psalm 16:11, 7:6-7, 47:2, 50:1-3, 68:1, 68:4, 82:8, 77:13-14, 118:26-27 added. Brackets [person], [these things], [of any] removed.

choices.why: The section opens mid-list (the titles the initiates give the Son, begun in the previous section); translated from this section's words only.

choices.english: Christ is hymned as uncreated God
choices.why: ἀγένητος (one ν) is 'uncreated', not ἀγέννητος 'unbegotten'; Didymus does not call the Son unbegotten.

choices.term: ιεʹ, ζʹ, μϛʹ, μθʹ, ξζʹ, παʹ, οϛʹ, ριζʹ, βʹ
choices.why: Greek Psalm numbers converted to English numbering in the reading text, each checked by verse wording.

choices.english: The Lord is a great God
choices.why: The predicate order of Greek Psalm 94:3 and 117:27 as Didymus quotes them; 27.12 then takes up 'great God' as a title.

choices.english: when he says “Arise”: arise to your ineffable incarnation
choices.why: Didymus glosses the prayer in the second person; the repeated 'arise' carries his paraphrase without a bracket.

choices.term: «τὰ μὲν ἔθνη τῇ πίστει κυκλώσει σε …»
choices.english: “The nations will surround you by faith; and you, return …”
choices.why: Didymus' own paraphrase of Psalm 7:7 set in quotation form; no reference given because it is not the verse's wording. The stray raised dot after τῆς is copy-text punctuation.
Didymus' epithet for David; kept as a title.

choices.english: him who rides upon the west
choices.why: δυσμαί is both 'settings' and 'west'; Didymus explains it in 27.8 as the last times, so 'west' is kept in both places.

choices.english: with good reason … blessed … without reason
choices.why: Didymus' wordplay kept as closely as English allows.

choices.term: ἀρχὴ ἐπὶ τοῦ ὤμου αὐτοῦ / ἑαυτοῦ ἀρχὴ
choices.english: whose rule is upon his shoulder / the rule, the very beginning, … his own beginning
choices.why: ἀρχή means both rule and beginning; Didymus reads Isaiah's 'rule' as the 'beginning' of the Son's human birth, so both senses are given in 27.22.
ἄρευστος: without flux or bodily change; the usual patristic word for an impassible birth.

choices.term: λαῶν 30 συνήχθησαν; ποι ῶν; ἐπέ φανεν
choices.why: 30 is a printed page number; the other two are words split across printed lines; debris, skipped or read whole.
